summary: Benfotiamine is a synthetic, lipid-soluble derivative (prodrug) of thiamine (vitamin B1) with markedly higher oral bioavailability than water-soluble thiamine. It is used as a supplement for thiamine deficiency and is widely employed for symptomatic diabetic and alcoholic polyneuropathy. It raises intracellular thiamine and thiamine diphosphate, activating transketolase and diverting toxic glycolytic metabolites away from pathways implicated in hyperglycemic tissue damage. It is generally well tolerated and is regulated mostly as a supplement/EU product rather than an FDA-approved drug.
indications: Treatment and prevention of thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, including in malabsorption or alcoholism
Symptomatic treatment of alcoholic neuropathy and other thiamine-responsive neuropathies

dosage.n: Often 50-100 mg per dose; higher initial doses sometimes used

admin: Being lipid-soluble, it is absorbed more completely than ordinary thiamine salts
For neuropathy, continued use over weeks to months is usual before assessing benefit
moa: Benfotiamine is a lipophilic S-acyl thiamine prodrug that, after intestinal absorption, is dephosphorylated to S-benzoylthiamine and converted to free thiamine and then to the active coenzyme thiamine diphosphate (TPP). Higher lipid solubility gives greater bioavailability and tissue thiamine levels than water-soluble thiamine. TPP is a cofactor for transketolase; increasing transketolase activity diverts glucose-derived metabolites (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, fructose-6-phosphate) into the pentose phosphate pathway, reducing flux through pathways (advanced glycation end-products, hexosamine, protein kinase C, polyol) implicated in hyperglycemia-induced tissue and nerve damage.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to benfotiamine or thiamine
relative: History of allergic reaction to parenteral thiamine

preg: Thiamine requirements increase in pregnancy. Benfotiamine at nutritional/supplemental doses is generally considered acceptable; very high doses lack adequate study. Use as clinically indicated.
lact: Thiamine is a normal constituent of breast milk. Benfotiamine at usual supplemental doses is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required at usual supplemental doses; thiamine is water-soluble after conversion and excess is renally excreted.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required.

interactions.food: Take with food; absorption is good due to lipid solubility
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol impairs thiamine status; benfotiamine may help correct alcohol-related deficiency
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory interference at usual doses

rare: Anaphylaxis (very rare, mainly historically with parenteral thiamine)

pearls: Not an FDA-approved drug in the US (marketed as a dietary supplement; available as a medicine in the EU/India) - record based on EU/SmPC and clinical literature
Far higher bioavailability than water-soluble thiamine due to lipid solubility
Activates transketolase, shunting glycolytic intermediates away from damaging pathways - rationale for use in diabetic neuropathy
Excellent safety profile; serious adverse effects are rare
missed: If a dose is missed, take it when remembered. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue the usual schedule - do not double up.
overdose: Benfotiamine has a wide safety margin; excess thiamine is largely excreted in the urine. Overdose is unlikely to cause serious toxicity. Management, if needed, is supportive; discontinue and treat any hypersensitivity reaction symptomatically.
